considered: mold as the linker, nextest as the runner, sccache for the Arch build, splitting the Btrfs job, a parallel reproducible build.
done: Baseline over eight runs: median 193 seconds wall and 20.0 job-minutes. The audit step alone compiled its own tool for 181 seconds; a prebuilt cargo-deny, a timeout on every job, cache saved only from main, a job that skips the heavy checks for documents-only changes, and no incremental builds brought a full run to about 177 seconds and 15.7 job-minutes, and a documents-only change to 61 seconds. A speed-up claimed for one job was cherry-picked from the best runs and was retracted in the log when the later releases overlapped.
rejected: mold: lld is already the default linker since Rust 1.90. nextest: a process per test would defeat the in-process lock. The others did not pay in measurement.
title: CI, measured first, then optimised

considered: Converting Markdown to reStructuredText with a separate tool afterwards.
done: The renderer builds each page once and writes it through a format object, so Markdown and reStructuredText are one class each; the default is unchanged (byte-identical on the template's real data), the output is validated with docutils with every warning an error, and the renderer, which had no tests, has ten. This repository is the first generated from the template to use it.
rejected: A second tool has two sources of truth; rendering from the data keeps one.
title: The text-as-data engine learns reStructuredText

considered: A linter configuration for every rule.
done: Each defect found by a read (a sentence written twice, a rule copied by hand, a boolean that was a noun) became a test that reads the source. Rules the code could not yet meet were recorded per file in a data file that may only shrink, so a debt is a list and progress cannot slip back. The last debts were paid the same day.
rejected: A lint rule cannot read the generated outline, compare a document with the code, or ask the project a question; an ordinary test can.
title: Rules found by reading become guards; debts become data

considered: Leaving it: it is only one line.
done: A hint added a few days earlier did not obey the option that silences hints; found by reading the documentation of the option. It obeys now, and the option says what it governs.
rejected: A new thing that lives beside an existing switch has to be wired to it; the switch's own documentation is where the omission shows.
title: The tip that ignored its own switch

considered: Declaring the kit complete because every test passed.
done: Ran the shipper, the timing report and the gate against this repository and fixed three defects (a workflow name matched case-sensitively, a gate that assumed where it lives, an unclear check message). The gate now runs as part of the tests, so it cannot silently stop working.
rejected: Every test ran on the project the tools came from; a tool that has not been run elsewhere has not been tested for being general.
title: The kit, run on a repository that is not its origin

considered: A line-count budget as the only measure.
done: Stopped judging progress by impressions: a structure-metrics script compared the code with each earlier release, and the first guards (a file is short enough to read whole, no print outside the presenter) were written as tests. The shipper and the fast gate were built the second time a step was done by hand.
rejected: Line counts alone: they are gamed by splitting a file without making it clearer, which is why the stranger test exists beside them.
title: Measure the real goal, and automate the loop

considered: More seeded reads.
done: Sampling modules stopped finding anything, so the program was run on a real fixture and every word read: a preview that spent two of three numbers on zeros, a first snapshot that never said what its restore point was called, a header showing a retired word. A terminal UI was driven through a pseudo-terminal and its screens printed.
rejected: They returned modules already read; the defects were in what the program says, which only using it shows.
title: Using the program as a newcomer would

considered: Reading more modules.
done: Six seeded cold reads each found real issues (stale words, a rule copied in five places, a distinction the code made and never named); a scan for repeated code found them all at once, and a second mode, which forgets names and numbers and compares only shape, found a rule that had been copied and renamed.
rejected: Reading finds one at a time and stops paying once a seed returns what has been read; a scan is cheap and complete.
title: Seeded reads, and scans for what reading finds one at a time

considered: Re-running by hand each time.
done: A package-repository job failed with an HTTP 500 while downloading the release's own assets. The failed job was re-run and completed the release; the download script retries five times now.
rejected: That is the repeated hand-work the playbook says to automate.
title: A release failed on GitHub's own error

considered: Releasing on a timer; releasing every merge but skipping verification.
done: A release per merge cost about eight minutes of waiting and gave users a version every few minutes. The release pull request already collects changes, so the shipper stops merging it each time: it releases at ten changes that make a changelog entry, a week of waiting, a change to packaging or the release workflows, or on request. The policy is a small function with ten tested cases, proven to fail when the threshold is off by one.
rejected: A timer releases nothing when nothing changed and everything at once when much did; skipping verification removes the only proof of publishing.
title: Releases are batched, not one per merge

considered: Retrying a failed spawn.
done: A test spawned scripts it had just written and CI hit text-file-busy. Put every spawn and every script write behind one lock; a stress test with 16 threads and 4 CPU burners failed 120 of 120 runs before and 0 of 120 after. Wrote down that 740 clean runs on a fast machine are weak evidence against a rare race.
rejected: A retry hides real contention and teaches the tests nothing; marking the test flaky would have buried the cause.
title: Main's CI failed on the race I had measured away

considered: Leaving the page as written.
done: The idea page said the adapters were the part least like the ideal. Reading each by its first line showed the opposite. The page was corrected, and the log says that I had guessed and was wrong.
rejected: A document that claims how close the code is to the ideal and is not checked against the code is the first thing to rot.
title: A guess written as fact, corrected

considered: Linking to snapall's files for the missing pieces.
done: Compared the template's own agent instructions with this repository's: the data rules had lost their reasons, the recipes and the rationale were gone, and the rule that a factual claim needs a source was not enforced (18 of 34 practices cited nothing). Restored them, and added an invariant that every practice cites a source. Compared the kit with the work it came from and found it missing: the catalogue of guards as functions and the architecture guard that wires them up, structure metrics, a screen driver for terminal programs, the lexer-based splitter and renamer, the starting files (agent notes, idea page, log, plan, pull-request body), and CI, release and dependency configuration with the measured levers. All added, with tests; each generalised tool was compared with its original on the project it came from, and every difference was explained.
rejected: A reader of the playbook who wants to start a project should not have to read another project to find the templates; links go stale and the playbook must stand alone.
title: An audit of this repository against everything done in the chat

considered: Layering the core by technical role (ports, adapters, services), which is the usual hexagonal layout.
done: Rebuilt the core as folders named for what the program is for, wrote one command as a worked example of the idea, and made the commands read as stories of named steps.
rejected: Folders named for patterns: they explain the architecture, not the program, and a newcomer learns nothing about what the program is for.
title: The idea: every layer is the top of the layers beneath it

considered: Leaving the idea in the canon and a reading list.
done: Nothing in the repository said in plain words what the code was trying to be. Wrote one page that does: the idea, one request followed from the front door to the machine, how to tell it is healthy, and an honest account of how close each part is to the ideal.
rejected: A newcomer finds well-organised code with no one telling them why it reads the way it does.
title: Telling the reader the idea

considered: Leaving the dates: nothing depended on them.
done: While preparing this playbook from the development log, 51 of its 52 headings turned out to carry dates counted forward a day per entry; git said all the work was done in about eight days. They were corrected from git history, the log says so, and the agent notes now say an entry's date is today's date from the clock.
rejected: A record with invented dates cannot be trusted for anything else in it.
title: The log's dates were invented

considered: Copying the scripts across unchanged, with a note that they were written for another project.
done: The shipper, the scans, the sampler, the gate, golden output and the CI report were made language- and project-neutral, and the ratchet, the outline and the findability ranking were ported to Python with tests. The sampler picks exactly the same modules as the original for the same seed. The duplicate scan matched the original's results (11 exact and 223 near runs) once given the original's exact notion of a trivial line, which showed the one remaining difference was deliberate (it also ignores closers like `});`). Golden output refuses to record a program that cannot be found or prints nothing, and a refused recording changes nothing. Three mutations of the guards were each caught by tests. The repository's own outline answers 11 real questions about its own scripts within the top three.
rejected: A copy hard-codes the first project's names, paths and release workflows, so the second project would start by editing a script it did not write; settings and options keep one script.
title: The kit is generalised, and tested on itself

considered: Checking the diff by eye.
done: Renamed 79 uses of a wrong word. Two regex attempts changed a JSON key and a fake tool's raw-string output without any test noticing; a lexer-based renamer that follows string interpolation and verifies that no string literal changed left all 65 hunks right, and a guard now keeps the word out of identifiers.
rejected: Eyes miss a one-character change in a long string; the property to check is that no literal changed, so the tool checks that.
title: The retired word, seventy-nine times, and a rename that lied

considered: Sphinx, which adds a theme, a navigation tree and search.
done: Added a static-site builder (tools/build_site.py) that turns every .rst file into a page with docutils, rewrites links between pages, and fails the build on a link to a file that is not a page or an anchor that is not on its page; 21 pages and 99 links checked. It has seven tests, including that a broken link stops the build, and the anchor check was shown to be needed by switching it off. A workflow deploys it to GitHub Pages on every push to main, and CI builds it on every pull request.
rejected: Sphinx would read the generated pages' plain links to .rst files as external, broken links, and adds a dependency and a configuration to maintain; docutils alone is the reference implementation and needs only a link rewrite. It stays an option if search is ever wanted.
title: There was no site, and I had said there would be

considered: Assuming the engine pull would cover the whole change here, since it covered it cleanly elsewhere.
done: git subrepo pull brought the generic engine's definition-list render.py update cleanly, but this repo keeps its own local tools/render.py (deliberately, for its richer presentation), so the pull alone did nothing here - the same bold-to-definition-list edit had to be hand-applied to all 8 spots in this repo's own renderer. Added the matching _config.yml, _layouts/default.html and assets/css/style.css by hand too, since those are not vendored.
rejected: Checked rather than assumed: grepped for bold markers in this repo's render.py right after the pull and found 8 still there, confirming the two repos needed genuinely different amounts of work for the same visual change.
title: Adopted the RFC-like minimal style, engine part pulled and local part hand-ported

done: Moved dc.py, render.py and the invariant checks into a new template repo once they had been battle-tested here, then adopted that template's engine back into this repo via .tad/, keeping this repo's own render.py local since its output (grouped principles, "Watch out:", "Also known as:") is genuinely specific to this content.
title: Extracted the proven tooling into text-as-data-template, then adopted it back

done: Followed the same migration as text-as-data-template once subrepo was tested and adopted there.
title: Migrated the vendored engine from git subtree to git subrepo

considered: Keep using the original repo as-is.
done: Renamed the original repo to software-engineering-canon-legacy, generated a new software-engineering-canon from the template via GitHub's actual template-generation API (not simulated), bootstrapped .tad/ with bin/adopt-engine.sh, and carried the real content and this custom render.py across - a battle test of the whole template pipeline end to end, at the request of the person running this project.
rejected: The point was specifically to prove a fresh repo generated from the template works for real, not simulated - this repo became that test.
title: Rebuilt this repo from a fresh generation of text-as-data-template

done: Web-researched sourced principles (DRY, KISS, parse-dont-validate, hexagonal architecture, etc.) and committed the first 15 principles, 8 architectures and 6 practices as a private GitHub repo (grenudi/design-canon).
title: Researched engineering principles and seeded the canon

considered: Adding all sixteen rules of the source text as separate concepts. Giving the numeric bounds the status of rules. Putting the comments position in as settled. Adding a new principles category, which the schema constraint would have needed a hand edit for.
done: Added stratified design and screaming architecture, five principles and six practices, with 10 sources that were opened and read, 21 relations and their citations. The findings come from building snapall (a Rust snapshot tool) to the rule that every layer is a small language and that the code, not prose, is the specification. During the work the author corrected the first wording: front file and file length were written as two rules with two bounds, when the principle is that every layer is the top of the layers beneath it, so one module speaks one language and length is only a smell. The entry was rewritten before it was committed.
rejected: Rules as a checklist: this canon holds concepts and the source text keeps the procedure. Fixed size limits as the definition of a good module: they are alarms and the source project keeps them as ratchets for that reason. The comments position as a law: Ousterhout disagrees in the transcript cited and both views are recorded in the caveat.
title: Added the every-module-is-a-small-language findings from snapall

considered: Keeping the sixteen rules as the shape of the canon text, as a checklist beside the concepts.
done: The author preferred the principle to a numbered rule list. The source text in snapall was rewritten as prose around the two faces of a layer, and this canon now leads stratified design with them: each layer has an upward face (what it is for and the words it offers) and a downward face (a body in the words of the layers beneath), and a layer below is the top of those under it. The source project continued the refactor under it: a missing noun found by reading a story (Stopped), modules split by language (one per command, and a four-language adapter file into four), with its size checks relabelled as alarms.
rejected: A rule list as the shape of the source text: the rules are consequences of one idea and its alarms, and a list invites meeting them without understanding. The numeric limits as definitions: they find candidates and a short file that mixes two levels is still wrong.
title: Restated the small-languages findings as one idea and not a list of rules

considered: Recording the rename as a refactoring catalogue entry: it is a technique for proving that a change preserved behaviour, not a move in itself.
done: Added the practice of capturing a program's output before a behaviour-preserving change and comparing it after, with Fowler's definition of refactoring and an engineering account of characterization tests as sources, and the source project's pull request as the worked case: 81 names and about 2,000 occurrences renamed so that the core says area and location where it said config and subvolume, with 24 commands compared byte for byte. Recorded Approved as the noun found after Stopped, and a second case of prose drifting from code (the worked example in the source text, now tested to equal the source it shows).
rejected: Trusting the compiler and the unit tests alone for a rename this wide: neither sees what a user or a script can observe, and a variable renamed into a scope that already has that name changes meaning without an error.
title: Recorded what a wide rename and the next noun taught

considered: Doltgres, Dolt, gitsheets, GlueSQL.
done: Tested the format against this repo's real data specifically (not a toy example): schema changes, ALTER TABLE limits, a real semicolon-in-SQL bug, BLOB corruption, and 300k-row determinism on a real multi-core CI runner.
rejected: See tad-engine's and text-as-data-template's own session logs for the full comparison - this repo was the proving ground.
title: Spiked DuckDB + JSONL as the storage format on real content

considered: tad as a top tab next to Linux Phones.
done: tad's backlog and milestones written as tad data and exported through its mark, so the observatory shows how close tad is to being a rhizcut in every repository.
rejected: A top tab (it would crowd the overall look); tad as a template (a rhizcut instead).
title: tad gets a path of its own

considered: Interrupt collisions and missing LPASS votes as the hang cause (refuted or unsupported by the audits).
done: Audited the WCD937x patch on the lab machine (no IRQ collisions, no MMIO overlaps); proved on hardware that aoncc caused the boot hang; got SSH over USB on first boot (a preset beats Nura disable-sshd preset); found the ADSP crash loop and traced it to the sensor registry in hexagonrpcd. lab-agent: agent API, durable results, local-first monitor, GitHub budget fixes, ntfy notifications; surya-lab repo with DT audit and flash tools.
rejected: A Python API for agents (the CLI with stable JSON is the API); a second monitor command (one command chooses local or remote).
title: Boot hang found; ADSP crash loop found; lab-agent hardened

considered: Retrying the WCD test kernel with more variations; GitHub auto-merge for releases (a workflow token's merge starts no workflows); the initramfs debug shell for unattended tries.
done: devlab in lab-tools, for any phone from its manifest: reaching the phone, the safe test-kernel try (boot counting, a timeout that falls back to stock, proven live), provision, test, health and watch (a regression against everything that ever passed raises one board task; silent when well). Sound silently lost to Sxmo's loopback card as the default output: fixed by the speaker's UCM priority, and now a check. The tas2562 volume fixed (0 dB had muted the amps). sxmo-deviceprofiles repo. Board: states at a glance, waits that show themselves, mouse selection, real editing in the reply box.
rejected: The clocks as the WCD cause (pinned on: same failure); the reset pin's mux as the cause (fixed: same failure); boot-time dyndbg for module code (it reaches only built-in code); dmesg for crash counts (a ring overwritten within minutes - the journal is complete).
title: The conveyor in Rust, health that watches itself, the microphone narrowed

considered: Separate boards per project (labels on tasks chosen: one source of truth); a PR from the feed workflow (the org forbids it: verified data is committed instead); loosening the org policy for one feed.
done: Speaker stereo on surya (tas2562 slot-length fix + stereo UCM), verified by ear through PipeWire on Sxmo, Phosh and Plasma. Plasma: a saved mixer state and a tas2562 volume bug silenced the amps; found and recorded. The grand picture: tad-engine draws matrices, a 46-feature catalog against Android, iOS and Linux, the device grid, an automatic test suite whose runs are filed here, weekly feeds (the postmarketOS wiki claims, kernel work on surya), the research sorted into the orgs. The device lab: flash with the fixes built in, provisioning (packages, Wi-Fi), one phone library, an Sxmo device profile.
rejected: Guessing statuses for the Linux distributions (left unknown until tests and feeds fill them); PC-side depmod when baking in a module (it made Plasma boot-loop); trusting an image by its folder name (a reference image carried an old test device tree - fingerprints now).
title: Stereo speakers, shells, the grand picture, the device lab

considered: Trying common default usernames or passwords to get a shell.
done: Rebooted the phone out of fastboot (job 0003): it is Nura, not Android, so adb does not apply at all - the real access method is SSH over a USB network interface fixed at 172.16.42.1. Confirmed (job 0004): the interface comes up and 172.16.42.1 answers ping in about 3ms, so the boot itself genuinely succeeds. Port 22 (SSH) refuses connections. Checked (job 0005) whether that meant an encrypted root filesystem waiting at a telnet unlock prompt, the standard pmOS/Nura pattern - port 23 is also refused outright, not just silent, which rules out the simple disk-unlock explanation and means neither service is enabled on this particular install.
rejected: Guessing credentials against a real device is not something to do unilaterally, security concerns aside from whether it would even work; the honest and correct move is to ask whoever configured this install.
title: Nura boots and is reachable on the network; no shell access without credentials

considered: Reusing ideal-project-playbook's concepts/relations schema for this too.
done: Created linux-phone-oco/docs from text-as-data-template. Schema: devices, components, support_status (the matrix), device_sources, plus the template's backlog/session_log/sources. Adopted software-engineering-canon's RFC-like Jekyll theme verbatim (monospace, uniform heading size, definition-list field/value rendering, 72-character width) rather than inventing a new one, since it already does exactly what was asked for and is proven. Seeded one device (xiaomi-surya) and 19 components with status, citing only what was actually confirmed by search earlier in the session; everything not confirmed is marked unknown rather than guessed.
rejected: Concepts/relations model general, reusable PRINCIPLES with their relationships; a hardware support matrix is a different shape (a fact about one device and one component, not a principle), and forcing it into that model would be more awkward than a purpose-built pair of tables.
title: The docs repo: schema, style, and an honest first seed of what is actually known

considered: Attempting a fastboot boot or flash as part of this same session.
done: Ran the first two real jobs through lab-agent against the physical device: a read-only USB probe (0001, phone not connected at the time) and fastboot getvar all (0002, phone connected). Confirmed for real: product=surya (matches the docs repo's device id), unlocked=yes, kernel=uefi, secure=yes, serial fcbd04b4, and the full stock Android partition layout. Cross-checked against upstream: this device migrated from per-device pmaports packages to the generic qcom-sm7150 port (U-Boot + systemd-boot + EFI, March 2025), which changes the install/partition steps from the older device-specific instructions - U-Boot goes to boot, the pmOS boot image to cache, the rootfs to userdata.
rejected: The user mentioned the device already has something called 'nuria' installed or flashed, which does not match any term found in the sm7150-mainline/postmarketOS sources searched; flashing or booting anything before that is understood risks overwriting or being inconsistent with whatever is actually there.
title: The phone, for real: bootloader unlocked, product confirmed, two jobs run end to end

considered: Guessing the panel variant (roughly even odds) to save a round trip.
done: With no shell access to the existing install, the alternative is a clean reinstall. Found the pieces: U-Boot release 2025-12-02 (github.com/sm7150-mainline/u-boot), a Nura/pmOS edge build at images.postmarketos.org/bpo/edge/qcom-sm7150/, and the documented partition steps (U-Boot to boot, the decompressed boot image to cache, the rootfs to userdata). Two things block actually running it, both things only the device's owner can answer, not things to guess: (1) which panel variant this specific unit has, Huaxing or Tianma - the official wiki's own method needs adb logcat while booted into stock Android, which this phone no longer has, and picking wrong means a blank screen until reflashed with the other one; (2) whether to proceed with a destructive reinstall at all, given the existing install cannot be examined first.
rejected: Wrong is not catastrophic here (reflash fixes it) but is still avoidable, and pmbootstrap asks the installer to choose this explicitly, so the owner may simply already know which one was chosen.
title: A fresh-install plan, prepared but not run: two things only the owner can answer

considered: Rewriting every mention of postmarketOS throughout, including source titles and URLs.
done: Verified via search (the project's own governance document pmcr 0003, endoflife.date, and independent coverage in several languages): postmarketOS officially renamed to Nura on 2026-09-27, a post-cutoff event. Updated this repo's own prose (devices.notes, two support_status.notes) to say Nura, formerly postmarketOS, on first mention. Left untouched: source titles (they quote real external documents, written before the rename, under their real titles), and tool/package names (pmaports, pmbootstrap, the postmarketos.org and gitlab.postmarketos.org domains) - the rename announcement itself says those stay as-is while the transition completes, so rewriting them would be guessing at URLs and package names that may not have moved yet.
rejected: A source's title is a citation of a real document; it is not this repository's to edit, renamed project or not. Guessing at new URLs for domains the announcement itself says are still valid would trade a working link for an unverified one.
title: The distro is Nura now: postmarketOS renamed in September

considered: Translating the family's data here.
done: The Linux Phones grand view declared as data (its family, eight views); its own text translated into Russian in its own translations table, marked by machine.
rejected: That: each project translates its own data; a lens only its own text.
title: The first lens, and its own Russian

considered: Retrying the raw file server; translated columns inside source tables.
done: ocoeco gather (activity, releases, CI) and its reusable workflow, running in all eleven marked repositories; shared tables read through GitHub's API; the lens kind and lens.toml in the harvest; the specification grown to lenses (8) and languages (9), with the rule that a project translates its own data.
rejected: The raw file server (stale for minutes, 501 to empty files); API headers sent to raw files; anyone translating another project's data.

considered: Keeping the machinery in the observatory's engine; renaming tad-engine to ocoeco in place.

title: ocoeco founded: the principle, the specification, the core

considered: A longer cut; a smaller font.

rejected: Both: they hide the fault until the next longer title or language.
title: Words never overlap

considered: tad as a top tab; renaming tad-engine in place; the engine depending on ocoeco's code.
done: The path for every subject (three horizons, milestones filled by evidence, readiness earned in order); a page per project (how close, backlog, log, ideas); How we work from the canon; the observatory's family as its sub-views, ordered by the mark; ocoeco founded as the working system, its specification written, the mark, discovery and harvest moved into it - the engine is only the face; land waits for CI checks to appear; lab-agent guide teaches the living practices.

considered: Restructuring every formatting call for messages; translating the rendered HTML afterwards.

done: The architecture written; the mark (schema 1) on seven projects; the engine in Rust (discover, harvest, site); a scheduled run that discovers, harvests, renders and publishes; the site restructured around grand projects with honest tables.
